site_or_subject: CRU Large Energy Users Connection Policy Decision CRU/2025236
operator: Commission for Regulation of Utilities (regulator); applies to all new data-centre connections
record: CRU decision CRU/2025236 (12 Dec 2025) [as summarised by Matheson LLP; the CRU's own text was not located]: new data centres >=10 MVA must provide dispatchable on-site or proximate generation/storage at least equal to their Maximum Import Capacity (de-rated), separately metered and participating in wholesale and capacity markets, before ramping to full MIC; 1-<10 MVA sites need behind-the-meter autoproduction covering 100% of MIC; all >=1 MVA sites must source >=80% of annual demand from additional Irish renewables over a 6-year glide path. 'Islanded' data centres are stated to be not in line with national policy. System Operators must submit initial proposals for publishing locational capacity and constraint maps to the CRU by 31 Mar 2026.

record: The 2020 policy capped connected-capacity growth at 67 MW per year (670 MVA by 2030). record: [older: 2022] On 10 June 2022 the cabinet approved a draft decree (in force 1 January 2024, Stb. 2023, 492, per the Middenmeer receipt) barring municipalities from permitting new hyperscale data centres except in two areas: the former Eemsmond part of Het Hogeland and the Agriport A7/B1 sites in Hollands Kroon; the draft decree (2023 text, Barro art. 2.15.1) defines hyperscale as more than 10 ha and 70 MW or more, and exempts applications made on or before the 16 Feb 2022 voorbereidingsbesluit. The Eerste Kamer had adopted a motion on 21 Dec 2021 (35925 XIV, H) asking the government to have the Rijksvastgoedbedrijf suspend sales of agricultural land for hyperscale data centres.

site_or_subject: Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) data-centre PUE, heat-reuse and renewable obligations
record: EnEfG § 11 (statute text): data centres commissioned from 1 July 2026 must reach an energy usage effectiveness (PUE) <= 1.2 within two years of commissioning and a share of reused energy of at least 10% (planned 15% from 1 July 2027 and 20% from 1 July 2028; DIN EN 50600-4-6, with listed exemptions); existing data centres must reach PUE <= 1.5 from 1 July 2027 and <= 1.3 from 1 July 2030; electricity use must be covered on a balance-sheet basis by renewable electricity at 50% from 1 Jan 2024 and 100% from 1 Jan 2027; operators must also report to the Energieeffizienzregister fuer Rechenzentren (per the TUV summary). A government bill amending the EnEfG was still in draft when the Bundesrat gave its opinion on 10 July 2026 (BR-Drs. 388/26). Mainova (30 June 2026) reports Frankfurt's daily peak load exceeded 900 MW on 25-26 June 2026, up from clearly above 850 MW a year earlier, with grid capacity expected to more than double; the release does not attribute the load to data centres.

site_or_subject: Energy Efficiency Directive data-centre reporting database: first technical assessment
record: The Commission's first technical report (EY, Borderstep and AIT for DG ENER, July 2025) on the 2024 reporting period under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364 covers 770 reporting data centres, about 36% of estimated EU data centres; six member states had no reported data and five had fewer than three. Germany reported the most sites (335 of an estimated 456), followed by France (133) and the Netherlands (85); Czechia reported none of an estimated 50 and Ireland 18 of an estimated 123 (15%). The report gives per-site means rather than EU totals: renewable energy about 16.8 GWh; guarantees of origin about 12.5 GWh, PPAs about 5.3 GWh (median 0; the report flags a possible unit misinterpretation) and on-site generation about 0.04 GWh. The three component means are taken over different subsets of sites and sum to about 17.8 GWh, more than the total; as shares of that sum they are roughly 70% / 30% / 0.2% (derived). WUE could be computed for 458 sites and a non-zero ERF for only 67. The Commission's public dashboard (last updated 25 Sep 2026), read for its 'reporting period 2025' view, shows 773 data centres in 11 countries, total energy consumption of 20.7 TWh, 4.4 GW of installed IT power demand and 8,752,919 m³ of water input, with weighted averages of PUE 1.27, WUE 0.51, REF 0.84 and ERF 0.0236; by size band, very large data centres (90) average a PUE of 1.19 and very small ones (143) 1.52. Its aggregated 2023 and 2024 data were reported as 776 data centres in 18 countries, 6.4 GW, 16.7 TWh and a weighted average PUE of 1.36, with Germany the largest hub [press: DCD]. DG ENER's data-centre page states that a report on the 2025 period is under preparation, that the Commission proposed a common rating scheme on 21 Sept 2026, and that publication of its proposal on minimum performance standards is planned for Q2 2027.

site_or_subject: Metered electricity, water and generator fuel at 11 EPA-licensed datacentre installations, 2023 (part year) to 2025
operator: Amazon Data Services Ireland (9 licences), Microsoft Ireland Operations (DUB14/15), Equinix DB5
record: Each industrial-emissions licensee files an Annual Environmental Report with the EPA; Table 3 gives energy used in GJ by fuel and Table 5 water used in m3. For 2025, the eleven licensed datacentre installations whose reports the ledger has read give 14.79 million GJ of electricity (4,109 GWh), 53.6% of the CSO's metered national datacentre total of 7,663 GWh; Amazon's nine licences alone report 3,720 GWh (48.5%). In 2024 the same eleven report 3,585 GWh (51.4% of 6,973 GWh). The largest single installation is Amazon Clonshaugh (P1171-01): 3,673,332 GJ in 2025 (1,020 GWh, 116 MW average). Equinix DB5 is the only installation whose generators burned fuel on a large scale (see ie-equinix-db5-prime-power-gas-2024). At Amazon Grange Castle South (P1170-01), generators burned 1,689 GJ of diesel and HVO in 2025, about one hour of its 460.87 MWth permitted fleet at full rating. Water: 1,133 m3 at P1170-01 in 2025 (down 87%), 399,153 m3 at Equinix DB5 (cooling towers). No AER reports generator run hours. The eight Amazon 2023 reports cover part of the year: Table 3 sets out the energy used from the month of licence grant (June or July 2023) to December. Taking those months, the eight averaged 370.6 MW of load from mid-2023 to December, 377.6 MW in 2024 and 412.0 MW in 2025; counted from the date of grant (13 June to 19 July) instead, 2023 would be 398.5 MW. Part-year averages can also differ through the season alone. Between 2023 and 2025 average load rose at five installations (for example Cruiserath P1182-01 from 47.4 to 76.6 MW) and fell at three (for example Blanchardstown P1172-01 from 65.6 to 49.8 MW). Microsoft DUB14/15's 2023 report covers July to December and the construction of three data halls; Equinix DB5's does not state its period.

site_or_subject: Scotland: planning directions for datacentres over 50MW, and the Parliament's resolution on decisions, 2026
operator: Scottish Ministers; applicants named in the UK site list
record: The Town and Country Planning (Notification of Applications) (Data Centres exceeding 50MW Power Capacity) (Scotland) Direction 2026, made under Regulation 31 of the Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (Scotland) Regulations 2013 and in force on 17 August 2026, requires a planning authority, within seven days of the validation date, to send the Scottish Ministers listed information on an application for a data centre exceeding 50MW power capacity; the Chief Planner's letter says it 'applies to both new planning applications and any that are currently being considered' and will enable 'strategic oversight and monitoring of the progress of the pipeline of applications'. No end date is stated. The Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (Data Centres exceeding 50MW Power Capacity) (Scotland) Direction, in force on 17 September 2026 (Chief Planner letter of 16 September 2026), makes such development EIA development, defines power capacity as 'the total proposed electrical power available to the data centre, typically expressed in megawatts (MW)', applies to both new and existing applications and 'will be reviewed periodically'. On 17 August 2026 the Scottish Government also issued directions requiring EIA for data centres at locations in Fife and Edinburgh: for Auchtertool, application 26/01243/PPP, the Planning and Environmental Appeals Division records 'EIA Required' (case EIA-250-002), and the Government's release links an EIA decision for Wester Hermiston. Ministers recalled the South Gyle appeal (PPA-230-2794), which 'is currently being considered by Scottish Ministers'. On 16 September 2026 the Parliament agreed motion S7M-01177, Hyperscale Data Centres, as amended (For 80, Against 26, Abstentions 15). Amendment S7M-01177.3 (agreed: For 94, Against 26, Abstentions 0) asks the Government to report back on national planning guidance by the end of the calendar year and publish it within 12 months, and 'believes that no decisions on planning or consenting in relation to such applications should be made until this has been completed', for current and potential hyperscale data centre planning applications. On 8 October 2026 the Minister for Public Finance wrote to the Climate Action Committee that the Government 'does not anticipate any such applications being determined' by planning authorities before the planning guidance is issued, expected before Christmas 2026, and is 'closely monitoring live data centre applications and their intended determination timescales'.
